title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) to evaluate conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized-token equality, fuzzy 5‑gram overlap, provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy on a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample. The run used a single hosted LLM (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") and a deterministic NetOps verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed 300 episodes (150 item pairs) but, due to provenance-stable synthetic sampling (synthetic-netops: source_identifier) and shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), each item used one shared generation (model_calls_used = 150). No preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags were produced (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty; SHA‑256 recorded), and all baseline and guarded episodes passed the verifier (baseline = 150/150; guarded = 150/150). Paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). Crucially, the synthetic provenance and shared‑generation semantics (both recorded in archived artifacts) render this execution uninformative about contamination prevalence in web‑sourced benchmarks; we reconcile preregistration→execution artifacts, explain this degeneracy with archived traces, and give artifact‑grounded recommendations for audit designs that would be sensitive to real-world contamination.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly being proposed and evaluated for network operations (NetOps) tasks (intent→configuration, automated repair). For operational trustworthiness, benchmarked performance must reflect genuine generalization rather than dataset contamination (items or templated prompts appearing in training corpora) or excessive templating that simplifies the task. Recent surveys and benchmark studies call for contamination-aware evaluations and verifier‑backed oracles to bound inflated claims of reliability.

Research question and contribution. We preregistered and executed an artifact‑anchored audit to answer: given conservative deterministic detectors (exact token equality after canonicalization; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance timestamp heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence contamination flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change an LLM's verifier pass rate? Our contributions are: (1) a complete preregistered confirmatory experiment (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) executed end‑to‑end and archived; (2) artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics for Npairs = 150 with detailed deterministic verifier traces; and (3) a preregistration→execution reconciliation that explains why this run produced a degenerate null and prescribes artifact‑grounded audit design changes to increase sensitivity in future studies.

Bounded inference and prominent caveat. The executed sample was generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). Both facts are recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl (artifact SHAs archived). Because of these two execution facts, baseline and guarded episodes reused identical model outputs whenever no high‑confidence exclusions occurred; this collapse made the prespecified paired test uninformative for generation‑level contamination detection in this run. We state this prominently to avoid overgeneralization: the observed zero‑flag and zero‑difference outcome pertains to this synthetic, shared‑generation regime and does not imply the absence of contamination in independent web‑sourced benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluations and agentic repair. Recent system and benchmark work demonstrates that LLMs can produce plausible configuration artifacts in constrained settings and that integrating verifiers or iterative validate–repair loops improves average repair quality compared to naive generation [https://openalex.org/W7157506260, https://openalex.org/W7163636922, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.22092]. These studies motivate our use of a deterministic verifier as an oracle and our focus on validator‑measured pass rates rather than superficial textual matching.

Contamination and construct validity critiques. Surveys of LLM evaluation highlight two recurring risks: contamination (benchmark items leaking into model training corpora) and construct invalidity (overly templated tasks that underrepresent operational difficulty) [https://openalex.org/W4404534210, https://openalex.org/W7166900660]. Proposed defenses include exact matching, n‑gram overlap detectors, provenance tracing, paraphrase‑robust checks, and human adjudication. Our audit implements a conservative subset of these defenses (canonical exact match; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance timestamp heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy; the study evaluates these defenses when applied under the archived execution semantics.

Positioning. Unlike broader capability benchmarks that measure absolute model accuracy, this work evaluates whether a specific preregistered contamination control pipeline would alter verifier‑measured success on a reproducible sample under the recorded execution semantics. The novelty is methodological and artifact‑anchored: we preregister, execute, and reconcile the run with archived manifests, and we surface design choices that materially affect audit sensitivity.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The experiment preregistration (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest) defined the primary estimand as the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across item×model pairs. The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computes the paired estimate, exact McNemar two‑sided p, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistration specified conservative detectors, a guarded exclusion rule for high‑confidence flags, and deterministic replacement semantics when exclusions occur.

Detectors and guarded policy (archived preregistered rules). Detectors were: (1) canonicalized exact normalized-token equality; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 and sensitivity thresholds at 0.65 and 0.50; and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps to the model cutoff. The guarded policy deterministically excludes only high‑confidence flagged items (exact match OR fuzzy overlap ≥ 0.80) and replaces them by deterministic retemplating + topology augmentation sampled from the same generator distribution with fixed seeds; replacements require embedding‑similarity checks per preregistration. These detection and replacement semantics are archived in transformation_manifest.json and the preregistration artifact (SHA recorded).

Sampling, task generation, and critical execution semantics. The preregistration allowed deterministic task generators for reproducibility and permitted shared generation semantics. The executed run used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 to produce synthetic tasks (task source_identifier with "synthetic-netops:"), and execution_mode set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate). When no exclusions occurred, a single shared model generation served both baseline and guarded episodes for each item. These execution choices are recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version="gpt-5-mini") and execution/task_manifest.jsonl; representative artifact SHAs are listed in the Disclosure Statement.

Verifier and scoring. The verification oracle deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator traces archived) executes parse→state‑update→property checks and returns a binary pass/fail plus a detailed validator_trace (observed_touched_field_count, required_command_count, final_state). The preregistered scoring rule for intent→configuration tasks—full_intent_constraint_validation—requires the generated configuration to produce the intended final state while respecting workflow constraints; all per‑episode scorer outputs and traces are archived under execution/scoring with SHA references.

Planned analyses and sensitivity treatments. The preregistration specified the primary paired test and prespecified sensitivity analyses: (a) treating failed model calls as failures; (b) fuzzy‑threshold sensitivity at 0.50, 0.65, 0.80; and (c) subgroup analysis by templated vs realistic items. Power guidance noted a multi‑model design targeted ≈5 percentage‑point detectable paired differences at 80% power; single‑model single‑call designs (as executed here) reduce sensitivity and increase minimal detectable effects. All analysis parameters and logs are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and bookkeeping. Execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item rather than two per pair). Deterministic_reconciliation confirms: complete_pair_count = 150, n_11 = 150, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, and provider_call accounting consistent with the preregistration (artifact SHAs archived).

Contamination detector outcomes. Per the archived detector outputs, no preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred for the sampled items; analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged rows (file header only) and its artifact SHA is recorded. The detector workflow archived overlap outputs only for episodes that met flagging criteria or required replacement handling; since no high‑confidence flags occurred, the archive does not contain an aggregated distribution of per‑item fuzzy 5‑gram overlap scores to report. Therefore, consistent with the archived evidence, we report the documented absence of high‑confidence flags rather than inventing per‑item overlap statistics.

Verifier results and confirmatory statistics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA recorded). The primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All numerical outcomes and per‑episode validator traces are archived with artifact hashes as described in the Disclosure Statement.

Representative exemplar episode. A representative archived episode (pair‑000001 / task‑000001) illustrates the artifact structure and validator outputs: normalized_reference_answer and normalized_response are identical (four command lines), validator score = 1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION) with parsed_command_count = 4 and observed_touched_field_count = 3; full response, scoring JSON, and validator_trace are archived under execution/responses and execution/scoring with SHAs recorded.

What the results show and do not show. The archive‑grounded facts answer the preregistered methodological question for the executed sampling regime: in a provenance‑stable synthetic sample with shared generation semantics and the conservative detectors implemented, no high‑confidence flags were raised and guarded exclusions did not change verifier pass rates. The results do not speak to contamination prevalence in web‑sourced benchmarks, to paraphrase‑sensitive leakage, or to multi‑model settings. We avoid extrapolating beyond what the archived artifacts support.
sections.discussion:
Why the execution yielded a degenerate paired outcome (artifact explanation). Two archived execution facts explain the degenerate null. First, sampled items were synthetic and provenance‑stable (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; source_identifier "synthetic-netops:"), so canonical exact matches to public fingerprints and high fuzzy 5‑gram overlaps were unlikely. Second, independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate): when no high‑confidence exclusions triggered, a single shared generation per item was used for both baseline and guarded episodes. Both facts are recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl and jointly produced identical baseline and guarded outputs per item, mechanistically eliminating discordant pairs and rendering the paired test uninformative for generation‑level contamination effects in this run.

Reviewer‑requested detector summary statistics and artifact limitation. Reviewers requested per‑item fuzzy‑overlap summary statistics (min/median/percentiles) against the public corpus fingerprint set. The archived detector workflow recorded overlap outputs only when items met preregistered flagging criteria or when replacements were applied. Because no episodes met the high‑confidence threshold in this execution, the archive contains no per‑item overlap summary distribution to report. We therefore (artifact‑truthfully) cannot provide the requested overlap summary statistics from this execution; instead we report the documented absence of flagged episodes and recommend that future audits always persist per‑item overlap scores regardless of threshold crossings so distributions can be reported even when flags are rare.

Design lessons and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations. The preregistration and execution artifacts together imply the following evidence‑grounded improvements to increase audit sensitivity: (1) sample provenance‑rich, web‑sourced benchmark items (avoid exclusively synthetic provenance) so detectors can exercise overlap/provenance checks; (2) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded outputs are generated independently and cannot trivially collapse to identical text; (3) expand to multiple models and independent seeds to detect cross‑model contamination signals; (4) persist per‑item fuzzy‑overlap scores and detector diagnostics for post‑hoc reporting regardless of flags; and (5) incorporate paraphrase‑robust detectors and limited human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation directly follows from archived facts (execution manifest, deterministic_reconciliation, and analysis artifacts) showing how current choices limited sensitivity.

Operational implications for NetOps evaluations. For practitioners assessing LLM‑for‑NetOps claims, the audit demonstrates that verifier‑backed checks are useful oracles for functional correctness, but contamination audits must ensure sampling and generation semantics exercise detector capabilities. An audit that uses synthetic provenance and shared generation cannot reliably detect generation‑level contamination even when conservative detectors are in place. Verifiers alone do not detect contamination; contamination detection requires provenance‑diverse sampling, independent generations, and recorded detector diagnostics.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors on a reproducible 150‑pair synthetic NetOps sample. The run produced zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical verifier pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded); paired difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]; p = 1.0). This degenerate null outcome is artifact‑supported and arises from deterministic synthetic sampling and shared‑generation semantics recorded in archived artifacts; it does not imply the absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks. We reconcile preregistration→execution artifacts, confirm deterministic reconciliation checks passed, and provide concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations (provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation per condition, multi‑model scope, per‑item detector logging, paraphrase‑robust detectors, matched power calculations) to increase audit sensitivity in future studies. All experiment artifacts, validator traces, analysis inputs/outputs, and execution manifests are archived and their representative SHAs are listed in the Disclosure Statement below.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLM families, sizes, or proprietary training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in web‑sourced benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection used preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
